summary:
Space-Mate is an interactive interface which allows the efficient prediction of diferent landing moon sites  from a selected spaceport. It's based on a graphic engine supported by real phyisics models of the moon and the heart. 
Using the Horizon API, we obtained the relative position of the Moon with respect to the Earth; subsequently by means of a ray-tracing simulation, we evaluated the visibility from the Earth and we relied upon Moon Trek to acquire the lunar topography and discount landing sites without favourable conditions, retaining only the viable sites within the communications window whilst ensuring the distance between the launch site and the Moon was minimised. Furthermore, we utilised Kaguya MI/USGS data alongside SP/LOLA for the North and South poles to determine the weathering and relief of the site, there by narrowing the available options even further.

This tool is important because it provides a simple app that automatically calculates extremely difficult problems with a simple input such as selecting a space centre and a date, determining which of the zones of the lunar surface are the bests, providing a clear way to compare the sites and their properties.

You can enjoy our AppWeb in your own PC and Smartphone
details:
Space-Mate. An interactive WebMap:



The operating principle of Space-Mate consists of the following stages:

To begin, we linked the relative positions of the Moon and the Earth utilising the Horizon system. This enabled us to obtain the spherical coordinates of the Moon and link its origin to a Mobile reference system (SRM), whose centre is located at the geometric centre of the Earth. To generate the communications window, we established that the position vector modulus must be lowest, taking into account the time differential elapsed between points. Based upon this consideration, we actively evaluated Earth visibility by utilizing a light ray-tracing simulation, whilst a further ray simulation was employed to assess solar power generation potential.

Aproaching this test, further considerations were required. We utilised the Moon Trek tool to acquire the general topography; however, for precise calculations, we employed Kaguya MI/USGS data (which does not provide total coverage) alongside SP/LOLA for the North and South poles due to their different behaviour. We utilised this topography to determine the efficacy of communications and power generation at points situated within craters, depending upon the angle of incidence. Consequently, the application automatically discards sites where power generation or communications prove unfeasible, thereby retaining only the viable landing sites, which are indicated on the interactive map by an image of Spacy holding a flag. Subsequently, the user must select the date for the mission, and for each available day, the system displays the diferent potential landing sites alongside their estimated daylight availability, travel time, and distance, amongst other metrics. Furthermore, these can be compared with previously executed missions by clicking on the blue flags located on the Moon, each containing precise information regarding a specific mission and its actual coordinates.
We developed two modes of use for the application: a "general public" mode, which offers a more accessible interface, and a "specialised public" mode, rendered in real scale. Within this later interface, the true aspect ratio can be appreciated, and it is also possible to run a simulation of the relative movement during the communications window. Upon completion of the calculation for potential landing sites within the window, users may select from different visualisation layers:

a) A weathering layer.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"upload_image.21:37:49.351153" ]

b) An illumination potential layer, complete with its corresponding percentage (as previously explained).

IMPORTANT: If you are on the specialised public mode, it is additionally possible to calculate dust levels and thermal degradation. To achieve this, the user will be prompted to upload a JSON file containing supplementary data; the data upload format is detailed within the options description, alongside an exemplary spreadsheet. All these indicators have their own colour scale, which is thoroughly explained within the application.

Moreover, we provide the facility to download all mathematical operations executed for the positional calculations.

To ensure our application remains user-friendly, we have integrated a virtual assistant named SPACY, trained to address the most frequently asked questions, alongside a quiz designed to entertain the user whilst complex operations are being processed.

The primary benefits of our software include its simplicity of operation, computational efficiency, and the capacity to evaluate not merely the communications window and power generation, but also the thermal degradation and dust levels present at the site. Furthermore, we have prioritised user comfort, providing an engaging and educational experience whilst awaiting processing, and allowing queries to be resolved intuitively.

We are available in English, spanish, portugues, french and Italian

The application is predominantly developed in TypeScript (Ts), amongst other technologies. Artificial intelligence was utilised during the programming phase, but was strictly excluded from the ideation and problem-solving processes.

Our team addressed all proposed evaluation factors as follows:

IMPACT: We sought to optimise the calculation times and preliminary preparation required for a lunar mission.

CREATIVITY: We developed a software capable of calculating available landing sites with a high degree of precision, outlining the pros and cons based upon a selected date.

VALIDITY: All employed models are underpinned by robust physical principles.
